To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopic measurements of metabolites in the brain do not support the use of proton magnetic resonance for the early diagnosis of Alzheimer disease.
the absolute concentrations of metabolites in the brain of patients with Alzheimer disease do not differ from those of elderly controls.
there is no significant decrease of the neuronal marker N-acetylas-partate and no increase of the glial marker myo-inos-itol in patients with Alzheimer disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) for the in vivo study of the human brain.
the development and evaluation of novel magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) techniques for in vivo studies of brain metabolism in health and disease.
the use of magnetic resonance (MR) spectroscopy for in vivo diagnosis of Alzheimer disease (AD).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data do not support proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic diagnosis of Alzheimer disease at this time.

in vivo proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic data do not provide evidence for major alterations of neuronal density or viability in Alzheimer disease, at least not in the stage when the diagnosis is made.
the data are not in accord with a major neuronal loss in Alzheimer disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic findings of the parietal cortex in Alzheimer disease are not consistent with a major loss of viable neurons, but rather reflect the presence of mild gliosis and cortical atrophy.
proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) is a useful method for the detection of gliosis and neuronal loss in Alzheimer disease.
in Alzheimer disease, proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic findings are in accord with known neuropathology, but do not support a major neuronal loss.
The main takeaway from our work is that
proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic findings in Alzheimer disease are in agreement with known neuropathology.
the metabolic changes in Alzheimer disease are subtle.
the use of magnetic resonance spectroscopy to diagnose dementia is not a reliable technique.
